## Why this meeting

The database now has enough real, repeated field data to say something
concrete about how the system behaves, not just where things are
located. This document lays out three things worth 15-20 minutes of
your time: (1) what the database currently shows about the system,
(2) what the new NDEP records add, and (3) the statistical plan for
figuring out how often chloride needs to be sampled to track the
system in real time -- explained without assuming a stats background.

## 1. Current state of the Steamboat database

A few numbers to anchor the conversation: **1,600 water-chemistry
samples**, **269 wells**, and **304,659 temperature-logger readings**
are now in one relational database, spanning real field sampling
(2026), NDEP compliance records (2024-2026), and historical literature
data reaching back to 1950 (Sorey & Colvard 1992, Mariner & Janik
1995, Skalbeck 2001). The timeline below places the current
reactivation event against that full history.

```{r fig-timeline}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| warning: false
show_fig("output/figures/manuscript/steamboat_timeline.png",
  "Seventy-year context: natural terrace-spring flow ceased around 1987, stayed absent through at least 2000 (Sorey 2000), and the 2022-2025 reactivation culminated in the June 2025 eruption. Ormat's permitted field-wide injection-limit increase (May 2025) is flagged as a candidate, unconfirmed contributing factor two weeks before the eruption -- not a demonstrated cause.")
```

**Three real findings worth discussing directly:**

- **A stable ~1.5-2 pH-unit gap between injected fluid and the
  shallow groundwater network**, holding across three real monthly
  sampling rounds (Sept-Dec 2025, 14 sites). This looks like
  water-rock buffering along a flow path, which argues for thinking
  about this system as reactive transport, not pure conservative
  mixing, at least for pH.
- **The Na/K geothermometer estimates a hotter reservoir (154-256 C)
  than the quartz/silica geothermometer (52-127 C)** for the same real
  thermal samples -- consistent with a deep, equilibrated reservoir
  fluid that re-equilibrates silica faster than Na/K as it cools and
  dilutes en route to discharge.
- **Current chloride discharge to Steamboat Creek is roughly
  27-59 L/s** (poster average ~27 L/s; one real dated measurement,
  2026-05-01, gives 58.7 L/s), against a historical range of
  ~60-90 L/s for 2008-2016 and over 1,000 L/s reported in the
  1950s-60s. The system is discharging far less than historically,
  even accounting for real seasonal variability.

```{r fig-geotherm}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| warning: false
show_fig("output/figures/manuscript/geothermometer_comparison.png",
  "Na/K vs. quartz/chalcedony geothermometer divergence, averaged per well across 67 real geothermometer estimates.")
```

## 2. What the NDEP records add

Scanned NDEP field-sampling forms (U230 forms + the 2024/2025/2026
TFT compliance reports) have been transcribed into the database over
the last several weeks, turning one-off grab samples into a real,
roughly monthly time series across **14 sites**: six named
injection-side ports (Galena 1/2/3, SB2, SB3, SBHR) and eight shallow
monitoring/domestic wells (Soccer Field, Herz Domestic, Herz Deep,
Eich, NDOT, Boyd, Jeppson, Rogers).

```{r fig-u230}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| warning: false
show_fig("output/figures/manuscript/u230_timeseries.png",
  "Left: pH, injection ports vs. shallow wells, pooled across three real rounds. Right: Herz Deep's conductance rising vs. NDOT's temperature falling over the same three months.")
```

Two wells move in **opposite, uncorrelated directions** over the same
three months: Herz Deep's conductance rises about 60% while its
temperature stays flat; NDOT's temperature falls from ~76 C to ~61 C
while its conductance stays flat. Neither temperature nor conductance
alone is a safe universal stand-in for "thermal influence" at this
site -- worth a direct question to you about which parameter (or
combination) is defensible to use that way.

NDEP's own UIC permit records also gave a real injection
pressure/rate snapshot (one document, 2025-05-30) for all 12 named
injection wells, including one well (`23-33`) whose reported current
pressure already exceeds its own newly-authorized limit -- flagged in
the database, not resolved.

```{r fig-injection}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| warning: false
show_fig("output/figures/injection_operations/injection_pressure_by_well.png",
  "Historic-peak vs. current vs. newly-authorized wellhead pressure by injection well, per NDEP's May 2025 UIC permit.")
```

## 3. The chloride sampling-frequency plan, explained plainly

**The question:** chloride concentration in Steamboat Creek is the
best tracer of geothermal outflow, but lab chloride analysis is slow
and expensive, so it can only be measured occasionally (a few times a
month at most). Electrical conductivity, by contrast, can be measured
continuously and cheaply with an in-stream sensor. **If conductivity
tracks chloride closely enough, a continuous conductivity record can
stand in for chloride between lab samples.** The open question is: how
often does chloride actually need to be measured in the lab to keep
that stand-in trustworthy?

**The approach, in five plain steps (no statistics background
needed):**

1. **Start with a real, continuous conductivity record.** Two loggers
   have been running since July 2026 (one upstream/"control" at Rhodes
   Road, one downstream at Geiger Grade), recording every 15 minutes
   -- a genuinely dense, real dataset.
2. **Build a model that predicts chloride from conductivity.** Once
   enough real chloride lab samples exist that overlap the logger
   record, a simple statistical model (basically: "as conductivity
   goes up, chloride tends to go up too, by about this much") is fit
   to the paired data. This turns the continuous conductivity record
   into a continuous *estimated* chloride record.
3. **Pretend you only sampled chloride occasionally.** This is the
   core trick: take that estimated continuous chloride record and
   throw most of it away, keeping only points spaced a candidate
   interval apart -- say, one chloride sample every day, or every 3
   days, every week, every 2 weeks, every month.
4. **Reconstruct and compare.** Connect the dots between the kept
   points (linear interpolation) and compare that reconstructed curve
   back against the real, full continuous record. The gap between the
   two tells you how much error that sampling interval introduces.
5. **Repeat many times, randomizing the starting point (Monte
   Carlo).** A single test at "sample every 7 days" could get lucky or
   unlucky depending on *which* day of the week you happened to
   sample. So the test is repeated 200 times, each time starting on a
   different random day, and the errors are averaged. This produces a
   realistic, honest answer instead of one that depends on a lucky or
   unlucky draw.

The output is a simple curve: sampling interval on the x-axis, average
reconstruction error on the y-axis. Wherever that curve crosses an
acceptable error threshold (e.g. 5%) is the recommended maximum
sampling interval -- the coarsest schedule that still keeps the
chloride estimate trustworthy.

```{r fig-mc}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| warning: false
show_fig("output/figures/manuscript/sampling_frequency_error_curve.png",
  "Monte Carlo reconstruction-error curve: average error (with spread across 200 randomized trials per interval) vs. candidate chemistry sampling interval, with a 5% reference line.")
```

**Honest caveat, stated plainly:** this whole pipeline is built,
tested, and working end-to-end -- but it has only ever been run on
synthetic (made-up, but realistic) chloride data so far, because the
real chloride lab samples collected to date (2026-05-01) predate the
conductivity logger deployment (2026-07-15) by about 2.5 months, so
there's no real overlap yet. The method is proven; it just needs real,
time-overlapping chloride samples to produce a real recommendation
instead of a demonstration. That is the direct motivation for the
calibration sampling campaign proposed in the thesis (monthly
chloride sampling for a full year, starting as soon as possible).

## Questions for you

- Does the pH gap (injection vs. shallow network) support framing this
  as reactive transport rather than conservative mixing, at least for
  near-surface processes?
- How would you interpret two wells (Herz Deep, NDOT) trending in
  opposite, uncorrelated directions on temperature vs. conductivity
  over the same window?
- Does the Monte Carlo sampling-frequency design above seem like the
  right level of rigor for a thesis-scale calibration campaign, or
  would you want it extended/simplified before the real field season
  starts?
- Given real water-level coverage *inside* the Steamboat field itself
  is currently only 2-3 wells, what's the right first modeling step --
  a simple mixing/box model, or is it worth waiting for better spatial
  coverage?
